title: Fish, trout, baked or broiled, coated

content.title: About
content.content: Trout is a freshwater fish of the salmon family, prized for its tender flesh and mild flavor. When baked or broiled with a coating, it stays juicy while the crust adds a crunchy texture. The product is often used in health‑conscious meals because of its low fat and high protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Trout inhabits cold, clear rivers and lakes in the Northern Hemisphere.
Unlike many salmonids, trout usually does not migrate to the ocean.
Coatings may include breadcrumbs, flour, spices, and herbs, enhancing aroma during cooking.
Trout is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which are beneficial for heart health.
Culinary preparations often pair trout with lemon, dill, or a butter sauce.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Trout protein provides all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: These polyunsaturated fats help lower triglycerides and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Trout supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish contains selenium, phosphorus, and potassium, essential for immunity, bone health, and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Low calorie density
items.content: Baked or broiled coated trout remains relatively low in calories when prepared with modest oil.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including trout.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: Like other fish, trout can accumulate mercury and other toxins; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Sodium in coating
items.content: Pre‑made coating mixes often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked fish may harbor pathogenic bacteria; cook to an internal temperature of 63 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Trout can be baked at 180‑200 °C for 15‑20 minutes or pan‑seared with a little oil until the coating is golden. Serve with vegetable sides, a squeeze of lemon, or a light yogurt‑herb sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh trout refrigerated at 0‑2 °C in a sealed bag for up to 2 days. Frozen trout should be stored at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw frozen fish in the refrigerator before cooking.
